extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in political anthropology / comparative sociology; educated general public and scholars studying origins and stability of chiefs/kings
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the factors that promote or undermine the emergence, permanence, and effectiveness of political headship (chiefs, kings, emperors) across societies and scales of organization. The rubric covers succession rules, supernatural sanction, wartime origins, administrative delegation, and scale-related effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-line (patrilineal) succession enhances stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession in the male line 'conduces better than any other to its stability' and often accompanies stronger, more permanent political headship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual explanation: in patriarchal groups the 'sentiment of subordination to the eldest male' and the greater probability that a son will inherit the 'efficiency with supremacy' of a great warrior make male-line succession less susceptible to usurpation. Examples and contrasts: Ashantee ('the order of succession is the brother, the sister's son, the son'), Dahomey (male primogeniture), transitions among Aztecs and Peru (Incas) and parallels with Egypt. Use this criterion to evaluate whether descent rules favor coherent, continuous authority across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession increases permanence (vs election)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition from succession 'by choice' (elective) to succession 'by inheritance' tends to make headship more stable and long-lasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: many simple tribes initially choose chiefs (Aleuts, Comanches, Land Dyaks, Nagas, Chinook villages). Compound groups likewise are often first led by elected heads (parts of the Congo region, King of Ibu elected by elders). Where hereditary succession becomes established, headship is more permanent. Use historical/ethnographic evidence of inheritance vs election to gauge likely durability of political offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination or nobles' selection can break female-line descent toward male succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Where sovereigns nominate successors or nobles choose among royal family members, descent through females may be bypassed, producing a shift toward male succession and increased stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original observations: in Feejee a ruler 'is generally the son' of the late ruler despite female kinship; in Madagascar the sovereign 'nominated his successor—naturally choosing a son.' New Caledonia: 'a chief nominates his successor, if possible, in a son or brother.' Use evidence of nomination mechanisms or nobles' selection as indicators of transitions away from matrilineal succession and toward more stable male-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession fixed in family but not person implies partial stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A stage where rulership remains 'hereditary in one family, but elective in the person'—i.e., limited to a family but not to a specific line or individual—yields partial but incomplete stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Abyssinia ('hereditary in one family, but elective in the person'), Timmanees and Bulloms, some Java and Samoa cases. Use this criterion to recognize intermediate forms of stabilization where the royal household retains the throne but internal selection remains fluid, producing limited permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wartime origin produces temporary common headship
rubrics_metrics.description: Common headship often first 'results from a war, and lasts no longer than the war'—wartime commanders-in-chief are typically temporary leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and notes: Patagonians chose an ajw during general war; Indians of the Orinoco recognize a common chief 'only in times of war'; ancient Germany and the Sabines had central governments only in wartime. Use presence of wartime selection and lack of institutionalized succession to predict transience of supra-local headship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascribed divine descent or supernatural sanction greatly strengthens headship
rubrics_metrics.description: When a ruler is assumed to be descended from gods, is worshiped, or is treated as a deputy-god, his political headship attains much greater stability and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: ruler becoming 'a deputy-god' or possessing 'divine descent' makes headship most stable. Empirical instances: Inca (divinity inherited on both sides), Egypt (monarch 'representative of the Divinity on earth'), Tahiti, Kukis, Emperor of China, Japanese Mikado. Consequences: claim to divine status can confer ownership of land/people, unlimited will over subjects, and combine military, legislative, judicial and ecclesiastical authority. Use claims of sacrality/divine commission as strong predictors of centralized, absolute authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief as priest or divine figure consolidates more permanent authority than magical power alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler who is also chief priest or of divine descent gains more effective and transmissible supernatural authority than a ruler whose power rests only on personal magical powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text contrasts: while a cacique (Chibchas) may claim to 'leave him heir of all his sanctity,' this is exceptional; generally 'the chief whose relations with the supernatural world are those of a sorcerer does not transmit his relations.' Being priest-ruler taps higher-ranking invisible agents and tends to create a supernatural dynasty. Evaluate whether supernatural claims are institutionalized (priesthood, divine genealogy) versus personal magical reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/bureaucratic delegation both increases capacity and dilutes direct control
rubrics_metrics.description: As rulers govern larger, united populations they 'employ others' whose assistants become 'established heads of departments with deputed authorities'; these agents increase administrative reach but also reduce the ruler's direct control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications: organized officialdom helps manage more numerous affairs but 'often impedes, and not unfrequently defeats' original aims; via deputies the ruler gets information and executes orders but becomes dependent. Extreme outcomes include the ruler lapsing 'into a puppet' or being usurped by a chief deputy. Use presence of formal administration and delegation to assess both administrative capacity and risks of alienation of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession independent of capacity risks figurehead rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: When hereditary rules rigidly determine succession, possession of supreme power becomes 'independent of capacity for exercising it,' enabling regents or ministers to become the actual rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and examples: heirs may be too young, feeble, or pleasure-seeking; regents or chief ministers then wield real authority (Tonga, Abyssinia examples). Use indicators of strict primogeniture and lack of merit-based checks to predict possible takeover by deputies or regents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred character makes ruler inaccessible and dependent on agents
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler's sacredness or inaccessibility (derived from divine status or sacral office) isolates him from subjects so that 'all intercourse with him must be through the agents' he surrounds, reducing his ability to supervise and adapt commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Abyssinia (king sits unseen in council), Thibet (Grand Lama discovered among people then reappears; divinity implies disconnection from temporal matters), Bootan (Dhurma Raja vs temporal Deb Rajas), Japan (succession of elders/hiros). Use measures of ceremonial sacralness and limits on direct contact to assess likelihood of dependency on intermediaries and administrative ossification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaker cohesion and subordination in compound groups reduces stability of supra-local headship
rubrics_metrics.description: The cohesion 'within compound groups is less than that within simple groups' and subordination to a compound's central head is weaker than to local chiefs, making supra-local headships less stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: Dyaks (rarely does one chief gain acknowledged supremacy), Caffres (subjects more attached to their chiefs than to the king), Homeric Greeks, early European feudal loyalties. Use strength of local loyalties and social cohesion measures to evaluate resilience of higher-level political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical developmental sequence of political headship
rubrics_metrics.description: Political headship tends to develop in a recurring order: no headship → temporary wartime leader → elective headship → hereditary succession → supernatural sanction/divine commission → absolute ruler combining multiple authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's 'truth to be noted': successive phenomena in simple groups recur in compound and doubly compound groups. Examples span many societies (Chinooks, Patagonians, Mongols, medieval Europe, Japan). Use this processual model to situate a society's current regime and predict next tendencies (e.g., election consolidating into heredity; heredity acquiring sacral claims).
